questions.prompt: A catalogue lists 22 kg-cm of torque. Give it in N m. Precision 0.005.
A stepper is rated 150 oz-in of holding torque (1 oz-in = 0.00706155 N m). Give it in N m. Precision 0.005.
A gearmotor must deliver 0.35 N m continuously and has a stall torque of 1.4 N m. Give the fraction of stall torque used.
A motor has an 80 rpm no-load speed and a 6 N m stall torque at its rated voltage. Speed at a 2 N m load, in rpm. Precision 0.2.
A rotor of 3.33e-6 kg m^2 sits behind a 100:1 gearbox. Reflected inertia at the output in kg m^2. Precision 0.0005.
A gimbal motor with a winding resistance of 8 ohm is held still on 11.1 V. Stall current in amperes. Precision 0.01.
questions.explanation: At standstill the back-EMF is zero, so I = U/R = 11.1 / 8 = 1.39 A.

questions.prompt: A screw has a 4 mm lead and a 16 mm mean diameter. Lead angle in degrees, arctan(lead / (pi x diameter)). Precision 0.05.
Which statement about coreless motors is correct?
options: They cog more than iron-core motors because the winding is lighter.
Torque is smooth at low speed, but low inductance can make PWM current ripple heat the motor.
They need no commutation at all.
They are the only brushed motors that cannot stall.
questions.explanation: No iron teeth means no cogging, so torque is smooth at low speed; the low inductance, however, means PWM current ripple needs attention (maxon academy, DC motor, p. 6 to 7).

questions.prompt: Why is sensorless commutation a poor choice for a robot joint that must hold position or start under load?
options: It cannot drive three phases.
It produces too much torque ripple at high speed.
The back-EMF it relies on is nearly zero at low speed and at standstill.
It needs a gearbox.
questions.explanation: Sensorless commutation reads the back-EMF of the unpowered phase, which vanishes at low speed and zero speed, so it needs a special start-up and is meant for continuous high-speed use (maxon academy, EC motor, p. 26).

questions.prompt: An open-loop stepper is loaded above its pull-out torque at some speed. What happens?
options: The driver automatically raises the current to catch up.
It skips steps and the controller is not told.
The motor reverses direction.
The encoder inside corrects the position.
questions.explanation: The rotor loses synchronism and skips steps, and an open-loop controller, which only counts the pulses it sent, is not told (SparkFun, Stepper Motors; Oriental Motor).

questions.prompt: Compared with an inrunner of the same mass, what does an outrunner (external rotor) give?
options: More torque from the larger radius, at the price of a larger rotor inertia.
Less torque and a smaller rotor inertia.
The same torque but no need for a driver.
Torque only at zero speed.
questions.explanation: The force acts at a larger radius, so torque is high, but the large rotor diameter also gives a high rotor inertia (maxon academy, EC motor, p. 8).

questions.prompt: A smart servo lists 19.5 kg-cm stall torque and 5 kg-cm rated torque at 7.4 V. Which figure should size a joint that works continuously?
options: The stall torque, since it is the largest.
The rated torque or the performance graph, not the stall torque.
The sum of the two.
Neither: servos need no sizing.
questions.explanation: Stall torque is a momentary maximum; the Dynamixel e-manual says real performance is closer to the performance graph than to the rated stall torque. Use the rated or graph value.

questions.prompt: Why do legged robots usually choose a low gear ratio (quasi-direct drive) instead of a high-ratio gearbox?
options: High-ratio gearboxes cannot produce torque.
Low ratios are cheaper to lubricate.
Reflected inertia grows as the ratio squared, which makes a high-ratio joint stiff at impact.
Low ratios make the motor spin slower.
questions.explanation: Reflected inertia grows as N squared, so a high ratio makes the leg stiff and impact-prone; a low ratio keeps the joint backdrivable and lets torque be estimated from current (Wensing et al.).

questions.prompt: A worm gearbox has a lead angle of 3 degrees. Which statement is the safest engineering conclusion?
options: It will always hold any load at rest.
It backdrives at every load.
It cannot be driven by a motor.
It may self-lock, but add a brake if the load is safety-critical.
questions.explanation: Self-locking needs a lead angle below the friction angle and is never guaranteed (vibration and finish reduce it); where safety is involved Boston Gear says to use a positive brake.

questions.prompt: A seller lists a gimbal motor and a drone motor, both with a 35 mm stator. A friend wants to use the drone motor to hold a camera still. Explain what you would measure and why it fails.
rubric: Measures or reads the winding resistance (tens of milliohm for the drone motor against about 10 ohm for the gimbal motor).
Computes the stall current U/R and power U^2/R at the supply voltage and compares with the current limit.
Explains that near zero speed the back-EMF is zero, all electrical power becomes heat, and the motor must be chosen by resistance, not by its speed constant.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Choose a motor family and transmission for a lift axis that must hold 20 kg when the power is cut and for a quadruped knee that must survive jumps, and compare the two.
rubric: Lift: a motor with a self-locking screw (lead angle below the friction angle) or any screw plus a brake, accepting low efficiency.
Knee: a large-gap BLDC with a low-ratio planetary and FOC for backdrivability, accepting more copper loss.
Compares the two with one number (for example reflected inertia growing as N squared, or the 8 degree self-locking screw).
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: Two vendor listings advertise '30 kg-cm' servos at an unstated voltage and without a stated stall current. List what you would check before treating either as a candidate.
rubric: Finds the supply voltage the number was measured at, and checks it against the voltage the robot will really have.
Asks whether 30 kg-cm is stall or rated torque and looks for a rated or graph value, a stall current and a gear ratio.
Looks for backlash, resolution, protection limits and a real datasheet, and treats a missing resistance or current as a red flag.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
